explanations: terra: People are commanded to worship their Rabb who created them. The source's `na'budu` and Rabb image is made explicit as a creature's service to its creator-owner.

luna: This ayah says those who follow God's guidance need not fear or grieve; it makes following guidance the answer to the section's image of the lost and the led. | terra: Those who follow God's guidance have no fear or grief. The source's lead animal becomes a covenantal pattern: safety belongs to following divine direction.

luna: The cow here has not been yoked to plow or water a field; it is a boundary case against the section's tamed camel used for work and carrying. | terra: The selected cow is neither subdued to plough nor to irrigate, and has no marking variation. It is a close boundary case for the source's tamed, recognizable working animal.
terra: It names one who has “strayed from the evenness of the way.” This is a precise route-form of the source's escaped camel and its dallīn.
luna: God appoints Abraham an imam for people; the leader (imam) is a human counterpart to the source's dictionary forms for the herd animal that goes ahead.

terra: The simile describes a recipient hearing only a call and cry. Its animal referent is implicit rather than named, so it only tentatively parallels a herd that must recognize its caller rather than hear meaningless noise.
terra: The hady may not be cleared by shaving until it reaches its appointed place. The source's H-D-Y leading form meets its animal-offering sense: a herd animal has a directed destination.

luna: The prophet appoints Talut as king over his people; the human ruler named malik gives a specific follower-and-leader counterpart to the source's dictionary form for the herd's leading animal. | terra: Talut is appointed malik over a reluctant people. The source's M-L-K word-family as a front leader gains a human political instance.
terra: A sign confirms Talut's kingship. Beside 2:247's malik, public recognition of the leader echoes the source's identifying mark on a herd animal.
terra: Talut sets out with his troops and tests their drinking at a river. The king of 2:247 is shown actually leading a group through a water boundary.

luna: The Qur'anic mark (root و س م) identifies discreet poor people; unlike the source's camel brand that identifies an owner, this mark reveals the person's condition. | terra: Needy people are recognized by their sīmā. The source's recognition brand is transferred to a human sign by which a hidden condition becomes legible.
terra: God is Mālik al-mulk, giving and taking authority. It distinguishes the source's creaturely mālik from the one who owns sovereignty itself.
terra: Those who obey God and the messenger are with those God has blessed. It gives the source's an'amta a company formed by obedience to divine leadership.

luna: The source's dictionary form wasm is a mark by which a camel is recognized; this ayah names garlanded sacrificial animals, whose visible marker signals sacred status rather than a human owner. | terra: The ayah protects sacrificial animals and their garlands. The source's branding sign has a close ritual counterpart in publicly marked hady.

luna: This ayah describes trained hunting animals catching wild game for their human handlers; it puts the section's tamed animal and its unowned wild herds into one specific scene. | terra: Trained hunting animals are taught what to catch for their keeper. Their learned obedience gives a concrete counterpart to the source's tamed animal that follows a leader and serves an owner.
terra: Moses tells his people to remember God's favor when He made prophets among them and made them kings. Ni'mah and M-L-K appear together as bestowed, not self-owned, standing.

luna: For killed wild game, this ayah prescribes an equivalent from domestic livestock; it explicitly sets wild animals beside managed herd animals. | terra: An expiation is an equivalent offering from livestock reaching the Ka'bah. The hady word-family ties a concrete animal to an appointed, guided destination.
luna: This ayah distinguishes lawful sea game from land game forbidden during consecration; it marks a boundary between wild animals and the managed animals in the section.

luna: This ayah calls the garlands on sacrificial animals signs; like the source's mark on a camel, they identify an animal, but here the status is sacred protection. | terra: The sacred offerings and garlands are institutions through which people know God's encompassing knowledge. Marked animal offerings serve a public order rather than private possession.

luna: This ayah rejects customary categories of animals deliberately released from ordinary use; it contrasts an intentionally designated free animal with the section's camel that escapes and loses its known owner. | terra: God rejects invented named statuses for livestock. The ayah challenges fabricated claims that detach animals from the true owner's command.

luna: This ayah calls land creatures and birds communities and says they will be gathered to their Lord; it gives the section's wild herds a Qur'anic frame as animal communities. | terra: Land creatures and birds are communities, then gathered to their Rabb. The wild herd is not ownerless in the final sense: even animal communities return to their Lord.

terra: A person is bewildered on the earth after devils entice him, while companions call him toward guidance. It gives the source's isolated stray scene and a concrete counter-call to a leading guide.

luna: Abraham says that without his Lord's guidance he would be among the astray; this shares the section's request for guidance and makes dependence on a guide explicit. | terra: Abraham says that without his Lord's guidance he would be among the erring people. It directly makes Rabb the rescue from the source's dalālah.
terra: After listing earlier prophets, the Prophet is told to follow their guidance. The source's following herd gains a concrete chain of exemplary guides.

luna: This ayah describes people assigning portions of crops and livestock to God and their partners; it adds a contested claim of ownership to the section's marked herd and unknown owner. | terra: People assign portions of crops and cattle that God created to God and to alleged partners. It contests human redistribution of a herd whose true source-owner is God.
terra: Invented rules declare certain cattle and crops forbidden and some animals untouchable for riding. This is a direct boundary around who may redefine the herd's use.
luna: The source's dictionary entry says a lost camel is called ḍālla whether male or female; this ayah shows a contrasting rule that divides livestock by sex.

luna: This ayah distinguishes livestock used for carrying from other kinds and permits eating from them; it gives the section's useful herd a more explicit division of work and food. | terra: Among the an'am are animals for bearing burdens and for slaughter. It directly supplies the source's carrying mount and beneficial herd.
luna: This ayah sorts sheep and goats into male-female pairs; against the source's gender-neutral dictionary form for a lost camel, it shows another Qur'anic way of classifying herds.

luna: This ayah asks about male and female camels and cattle; it makes a specific contrast with the source's statement that either sex can be a ḍālla. | terra: Two of camels and two of cattle are named while false prohibitions are challenged. It keeps the source's camel within a dispute over who may claim authority over livestock.
terra: God's straight path is to be followed, while other paths scatter people from it. The source's single leader and a camel gone off alone become an explicit route-and-dispersal contrast.
terra: Satan vows to sit on God's straight path to obstruct people. The source's route is shown as a place where a rival leader tries to turn a following group away.
terra: A camel cannot pass through the eye of a needle before the arrogant enter the Garden. The source's familiar animal becomes a physical image of an impossible boundary.

luna: People on the barrier recognize others by their marks (root و س م); the identifying sign parallels the source's camel brand but signals a person's standing. | terra: People on the Heights recognize groups by their marks. Like the source's branded camel, an outward sign identifies a person in a decisive gathering.
terra: The people on the Heights recognize arrogant people by their marks; 7:46 establishes the sign-based recognition, and this ayah applies it to a named group.

luna: The she-camel is explicitly God's sign and is left to graze on God's land; this closely joins animal ownership, grazing, and a boundary against harming the animal. | terra: The she-camel is Allah's sign and is to be left to graze in Allah's earth. It joins divine ownership, an identifiable animal, and pasture.

luna: The people hamstring the she-camel after being warned to leave her; this is the reversal of the section's owned camel being kept and recognized. | terra: Thamud hamstrings the she-camel after their command to leave it unharmed. It shows a community refusing the owner-defined limit around the animal.
terra: Those who follow the messenger, support him, and follow the light sent down with him are called successful. It gives the source's following relation a revealed guide and a communal response.
terra: People are commanded to believe in the messenger and follow him so that they may be guided. It directly joins following a leader to receiving guidance.
terra: The man who follows desire is likened to a panting dog whether driven off or left alone. An animal image exposes a human who refuses elevation through the signs.

luna: This ayah compares heedless people to livestock and says they are more astray; it reverses the section's claim that an animal can lose its way while still recognizing its herd and owner. | terra: People who do not use heart, eyes, and ears are likened to cattle and said to be more astray. It states the source's reversal: a human can be more lost than the herd animal.
terra: Among the created are a community that guides by truth and acts justly by it. This supplies a collective form of reliable guidance rather than a lone animal leader.
terra: If idols are called to guidance, they do not follow. The source's leader-and-herd relation is reversed in a summons that produces no following.
terra: Rain produces vegetation eaten by people and cattle, then it becomes as if it had never flourished. The herd's pasture is provisioned but not permanent.

luna: The ayah asks whether one who guides to truth is more worthy to be followed; it states directly the leader-and-follower relation that the section draws from its dictionary forms for the herd's fore-animal and guide. | terra: It asks whether the One who guides to truth is more worthy of being followed than one who cannot guide unless guided. This gives the source's hâdî and following herd an explicit criterion for a true leader.

luna: The section's stray camel has no known human owner in a desolate place; this ayah says every creature's provision and settled place are known to God, extending care beyond visible ownership. | terra: Every creature's provision is upon God, who knows its settled place and repository. It answers the source's animal left in a desolate place with the encompassing knowledge and provision of its true owner.
terra: Every dābbah is held by its forelock while the speaker says, “my Rabb is on a straight path.” Ownership, the animal's leading point, and the route all meet in one ayah.

luna: Like 7:73, this ayah names God's she-camel and permits her to graze on God's land, making divine ownership and pasture explicit together. | terra: The she-camel is again Allah's sign, to eat in God's earth without harm. Its named owner and lawful grazing form the opposite of the source's unowned camel in wasteland.

luna: The people hamstring the protected she-camel of 11:64, turning the granted grazing boundary into its violation. | terra: After hamstringing the she-camel, Thamud receive a final three-day term. The ayah makes violation of the animal's protected status consequential.
terra: Joseph asks whether scattered masters are better than the One overpowering God. The source's Rabb as owner gains a monotheistic boundary: a herd cannot coherently belong to rival masters.

terra: Following 12:39's rival masters, Joseph says judgment belongs only to God and that people are commanded to worship Him alone. It gives the source's owner-and-service relation its exclusive object.
terra: The malik's dream stages seven fat cows consumed by seven lean ones. Kingly rule and a cattle scene meet, extending the source's M-L-K and herd vocabulary.
terra: Joseph's brothers find their goods restored and ask for an additional camel-load. The camel appears as a measured carrying unit within an owned provision economy.

luna: A king's cup is reported lost, and its finder is promised a camel-load; the verse gives a concrete lost-property scene whose reward is measured through a camel, contrasting with the section's camel lost from its owner. | terra: The king's missing cup is announced with a camel-load as the reward for returning it. A lost possession, its royal owner, and a camel burden meet in one scene.
terra: The Prophet calls to God with insight, “I and whoever follows me.” The ayah makes a guided way a visible chain of leader and followers.

luna: This ayah says every people has a guide; its guide (root ه د ي) parallels the source's dictionary form hādī for the animal going ahead of a group. | terra: After calling the Prophet a warner, it says that every people has a guide. The source's hâdî is thereby widened from a herd's front animal to a people-specific guide.
terra: Garments of tar clothe the criminals. The source's tar-treated, tamed camel is inverted into a human garment of punishment.

luna: The source's dictionary form naʿam (root ن ع م) names camels for the good they bring; this ayah uses al-anʿām and names warmth and benefits, grounding that link in the Qur'an. | terra: It explicitly creates the an'am for people with warmth and benefits, grounding the source's claim that herd animals are called na'am because they bring good and benefit.

luna: The source's herd leaves for pasture and returns; this ayah gives those two daily movements as a beauty for their owners. | terra: It stages the flock's evening return and morning release, the exact herd movement and beauty developed in the section.

luna: The herd's long-distance load carrying appears here, and the ayah closes by calling the Lord compassionate and merciful toward people using the animals. | terra: The animals carry burdens to distant lands, making concrete the source's mounted animal whose legs carry and the owner's merciful provision for it.

luna: The source's dictionary form hawādī names the necks or leading band of horses; this ayah names horses and donkeys as riding animals, though it does not itself describe them leading a herd. | terra: The next ayah broadens the section's riding scene to horses, mules, and donkeys made for riding and adornment before 16:9 turns to the way.

luna: The section explicitly connects its dictionary form jāʾir to this ayah's crooked ways; the passage moves from livestock to Allah's responsibility for the straight way. | terra: It explicitly joins the animal passage to a straight way and a deviating way. The source's dictionary form hâdî, the leading animal, gives bodily force to guidance and to the contrary route.

luna: Rain, drinking water, plants, and grazing livestock make this a direct pasture scene, supplying the setting for the section's settled herd. | terra: Rain produces trees in which people pasture their animals. It supplies the actual grazing act that the source's preferred merabb presumes.
terra: After the livestock benefits of 16:5–16, people cannot count God's ni'mah. The source's lexical move from an'am to benefit receives its immediate Qur'anic horizon.
terra: Every community receives a messenger commanding worship of God and avoidance of false gods; some are guided and some deserve error. It is herd-scale leadership with a real split in response.
terra: All moving creatures in the heavens and earth prostrate to God. The source's `na'budu` and tamed-animal relation meet in creatures whose submission belongs to their maker.

luna: This ayah draws milk from cattle as a pure drink, a concrete benefit that fits the section's explanation of livestock as bringing good. | terra: Milk from between waste and blood in cattle is a sign for drinkers, a precise instance of the good and benefit the source assigns to an'am.

luna: The source's dictionary form calls the leading bee the malīk al-naḥl; this ayah presents bees as receiving direction from their Lord, giving the bee-leader gloss a divine-guidance counterpart. | terra: The Lord inspires the bees where to make dwellings. It gives an animal collective a divinely directed habitation, relevant to the source's bee “malīk” and herd under a guide.

luna: The bee is told to follow its Lord's made-easy paths; this is a specific parallel to the section's bee leader and to the image of a follower taking a guided route. | terra: The bees are told to follow the ways of their Rabb made easy, then produce healing drink. The source's hâdî image becomes an animal following divinely eased routes that yield benefit.

luna: This ayah contrasts an owned, powerless servant with a person provided for; the servant word shares root ع ب د with the source's dictionary form muʿabbad for the subdued camel, while showing the human sense of that root. | terra: The parable contrasts an owned servant unable to do anything with one freely providing good provision. It makes the source's owner/dependent relation concrete while testing false equivalence with God.
terra: From livestock come portable shelters, furnishings, and wool, fur, and hair. It extends the source's animal benefit beyond transport and food.

luna: This ayah names the she-camel given to Thamud as a clear sign and says they wronged it; it adds another Qur'anic camel scene in which human treatment of the animal is decisive. | terra: The Thamud camel is recalled as a visible sign that they wronged. The source's identifying sign is here a sign-bearing camel whose rejection exposes human blindness.

luna: Every people is called with its imam; the ayah makes the section's leading animal and following herd a social image of followers gathered with a leader. | terra: Every people will be called with its imam. The source's front animal becomes a final-account image of communities identified with the guide they followed.
terra: Whomever God guides is guided, and no guiding protector is found for one He lets stray. It gives the source's lost creature an absolute limit on substitute leadership.
luna: The fish slips away into the sea during a journey; it parallels the section's camel escaping its owner, while the fish's purposeful route contrasts with the camel left ownerless.
luna: The companion admits forgetting the fish and reports that it went into the sea; this ayah supplies the remembered loss that leads to the return in 18:64.
luna: Moses recognizes the fish's disappearance as what they sought and turns back; this ayah completes the search around an escaped animal.
luna: Moses asks to follow a teacher who can guide him; this makes explicit the follower's request for a leader that the section draws from the herd's fore-animal.
terra: Jesus calls Allah “my Rabb and your Rabb,” commands worship, and names this a straight path. It tightly joins owner, service, and direction.

luna: Abraham asks his father to follow him because he will guide him to a straight path; this turns the section's animal guide and following herd into an explicit human-guidance scene. | terra: Abraham tells his father, “follow me; I will guide you to a straight path.” It is the human form of the source's front-running guide whom others must follow.

luna: Moses describes using his staff to tend his sheep; this adds a herdsman's practical care to the section's owned and guided flock. | terra: Moses uses his staff to knock leaves down for his sheep. It stages a keeper feeding a flock, behind the source's herd, pasture, and guiding animal.
terra: Moses and Aaron are told to announce peace for whoever follows guidance. It attaches a concrete promised outcome to the source's act of following the guide.
terra: Moses says his Rabb neither goes astray nor forgets. The source's lost/unknown camel is countered by a Lord whose knowledge never loses its object.

luna: This ayah gives roads through the earth and rain-grown plants; 20:54 completes the scene by naming the cattle that graze there, echoing the section's meeting of path and pasture. | terra: God makes paths through the earth, sends down water, and brings out paired plants; 20:54 then tells people to pasture their livestock. This ayah supplies the route and growth that make the next ayah's grazing possible.

luna: This ayah directly tells people to eat and pasture their cattle; the preceding 20:53 supplies earth, roads, rain, and vegetation, joining the herd's grazing place to a traversed landscape. | terra: People are told to eat and pasture their an'am. The paired human and herd feeding makes the source's merabb and pasture an explicit Qur'anic practice.
luna: The ayah says Pharaoh led his people astray and did not guide them; it reverses the section's good fore-animal who leads a herd along a way.

luna: God says whoever follows His guidance will not go astray; this joins the section's image of a lost animal and a follower needing a guide in one claim. | terra: Whoever follows God's guidance will neither go astray nor suffer. The source's flock follows a hâdî; this ayah states the consequence of that following against straying.

luna: This ayah calls prophets leaders who guide by God's command, a direct parallel to the section's dictionary form for the animal that goes ahead and guides the rest. | terra: Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob are made leaders who guide by God's command. This is the human counterpart to the source's leading animal whom the rest follow.

luna: A flock of sheep wanders into a field and damages its crop; the ayah places a straying herd under human judgment, a close counterpart to the section's escaped camel. | terra: David and Solomon judge a field damaged at night by a people's sheep. A flock that has ranged into another's crop makes herd ownership and responsible tending legally visible.
terra: Whoever takes Satan as ally is led astray and guided toward the Blaze. It is the anti-hādī: a leader whose following has the opposite destination.
terra: The arrogant person turns aside to lead people from God's way. The bodily turn makes a crooked front-runner the contrary of the source's guiding leader.
terra: Pilgrims name God over the bahīmat al-an'am He has provided and feed the needy. The herd's benefit is explicitly returned to its giver and shared.

terra: In the sacrificial-rites passage, benefits remain in the offerings until an appointed term, then their destination is the Ancient House. It adds duration and destination to the animal scene of 22:36.
terra: Every community has a rite for naming God over livestock He provided. It connects animals as provision with service to the one true God.

luna: This ayah names sacrificial camels among God's symbols and says they have been subjected for people, joining the camel image to divine ownership and service. | terra: Sacrificial camels are made among God's signs; they stand in rows, are named over, then feed both owner and needy. It is a dense Qur'anic scene of marked, directed camel use.

luna: After 22:36's sacrificed camels, this ayah says their meat and blood do not reach God but piety does; it limits what the camel offering means in relation to its divine owner. | terra: Neither the camels' meat nor blood reaches God, but piety does. Against treating the herd as an end in itself, it fixes the owner-directed purpose of 22:36's sacrifice.

luna: The source's naʿam link is benefit: this ayah names livestock, drink from within them, and other benefits for people. | terra: Livestock contain a lesson: drink comes from within them, they have many benefits, and they are eaten. This unfolds the source's na'am as practical good.
luna: The section's herd is a working possession; this ayah adds riding livestock and ships, extending the animal's role from pasture and benefit to transport.
terra: The Prophet calls people to a straight path. The ayah supplies a voiced guide in the place where the source imagines an animal leader at the front.
terra: God's hand holds the dominion of every thing, while He protects and cannot be protected against. This cosmic ownership supplies the force behind calling every thing's Rabb its mālik.

terra: Birds in flight each know their own prayer and glorification. An animal collective has an ordered response to its Lord, extending the source's herd-under-owner image without making birds livestock.

luna: This ayah describes creatures moving on bellies, two legs, or four; it gives a Qur'anic counterpart to the section's dictionary detail that a riding animal is carried by its legs. | terra: Creatures made from water move by belly, two legs, or four. The source's mount carried on its legs is placed within the Qur'anic differentiation of animal movement.

terra: After 24:45 differentiates animal movement, this ayah says God guides whom He wills to a straight path. It joins creaturely motion to the section's requested direction without conflating the two.

luna: This ayah also calls people like livestock, even more astray in the way; its explicit reversal sharpens the section's distinction between an animal and a human who will not follow guidance. | terra: It again calls heedless people like an'am, then more astray in way, making the strayness of the source's camel a judgment on human direction.
terra: Rain revives a dead land and gives drink to cattle and many people. It ties animal provision to the Lord's life-giving care behind the source's useful herd.
terra: Abraham says the One who created him is the One who guides him. The source's animal hâdî opens into the Creator's personal guidance of the creature.
terra: The same speaker says God feeds and gives him drink. Beside 26:78's guidance, this is the owner-provider relation seen in the herd's food and water.

luna: The she-camel has a designated turn to drink, with a turn for the people; this gives a concrete water boundary around an animal that grazes on land. | terra: Salih assigns the she-camel one drinking day and the people another known day. It is a precise pasture-and-water order for a divinely owned animal.
luna: The command not to harm the she-camel sets a boundary around the animal placed in human care, reversing the runaway camel's loss from its owner.

luna: After the she-camel's protected drinking turn, the people hamstring her; the animal's allotted place is violently broken. | terra: They hamstring the camel and become regretful. The act turns the source's cared-for, useful herd animal into the focus of breached trust.
luna: Solomon's human, jinn, and bird forces are gathered in ranks; this supplies a Qur'anic scene of a leader arranging a group that includes animals.

luna: One ant warns the other ants to enter their homes, giving the section's bee leader and following group a direct animal parallel of a guide directing its community. | terra: An ant warns its community to enter their dwellings before Solomon's forces arrive. Like the source's bee and herd details, it stages an animal community receiving a protective lead from within.
luna: Solomon checks the birds and notices the hoopoe is missing; this is a specific scene of an animal absent from its leader's ordered company.
luna: The hoopoe returns with news after being missing in 27:20; its own contribution is the animal's return to the leader, completing the loss-and-return scene.
terra: Moses sets out toward Madyan asking his Lord for a sound way; the next scene, 28:23, brings him to the watering flocks. The traveler's request leads into a pastoral encounter.

luna: Moses finds women holding back their flock until the shepherds water theirs; this gives the section's herd a human keeper and a shared watering scene. | terra: At Madyan, two women hold their flocks back at the water until the shepherds leave. The ayah gives a precise herd, keeper, waiting place, and watering boundary.

luna: Moses waters the women's flock after meeting them in 28:23; this ayah supplies the act of care that completes that shepherd-and-herd scene. | terra: Moses waters the two women's animals; 28:23 supplies the flock, and this ayah's own act is the keeper's relief of its need at the watering place.
luna: This ayah calls rulers leaders to the Fire; it is the opposite of the section's guide whose followers are led toward the straight path.

luna: The ayah says many creatures do not carry their own provision and that God provides for them; it offers a specific counterpart to the camel stranded without a known owner. | terra: Many creatures do not carry their own provision, yet God provides for them and for people. It gives the source's animal dependence a wider providential frame.

terra: The parable asks whether people would accept those their right hands possess as equal partners in provision. It uses ownership dependency to reject divided lordship, like the source's single herd owner.

luna: This ayah likewise describes leaders who guide by God's command; it adds patience and certainty as the qualities behind sound leadership. | terra: Leaders from the Children of Israel guide by God's command while they are steadfast. It specifies what a valid guide at the front of a community is like.
terra: Water is driven to barren land so crops feed both cattle and people. The ayah makes pasture a supplied destination for a herd, not merely scenery.

luna: People blame their chiefs for leading them astray; it gives the follower's consequence when the section's guide-and-herd relation fails. | terra: The condemned say they obeyed masters and great ones, who led them astray from the path. It is a direct false-leader version of the herd's following.
luna: This ayah joins praise (ḥamd) to God's ownership of what is in the heavens and earth; it frames the source's liked pasture and humanly ownerless camel within divine ownership.
terra: The ayah notices varied colors among beasts and livestock. It offers an indirect natural counterpart to the source's visible identifying mark, though color here is not an ownership brand.
terra: A man comes running from the far end of the city and says, “Follow the messengers.” The movement and summons dramatize a community needing a guide.
terra: He tells them to follow those who ask no payment and are rightly guided. 36:20 provides the summons; this ayah identifies the followers' trustworthy lead.
terra: “Worship Me; this is a straight path” joins the source's `na'budu` root to its `ihdinā` route: service to the true owner is the path rather than ownerless wandering.

luna: The section says a herd belongs to an owner; this ayah says people are made owners of livestock, using mālikūn for that relation. | terra: It says God made the an'am and that people are their mālikūn, directly matching the source's Rabb/mālik relation to a herd.

luna: This ayah says the livestock were subdued for people, a direct counterpart to the section's dictionary description of the tar-coated camel as tamed. | terra: The cattle are made compliant, ridden, and eaten. This is the Qur'anic counterpart to the source's tamed mount and its useful service.

luna: This ayah completes the same livestock passage with further benefits and drink, giving a concrete instance of the good associated with the source's naʿam. | terra: Benefits and drinks come from the same tamed animals, completing the source's account of the herd as ni'mah-bearing provision.
terra: The dominion of every thing is in God's hand and all return to Him. It completes 36:71's human ownership of cattle with God's prior ownership of all things.
terra: The wrongdoers are gathered with those like them and what they worshipped. Its gathering language begins a contrary herd movement toward judgment.
terra: The angels are told to guide them to the path of Hell. Following 37:22's gathering, this is a terrible inversion of the source's sought-after guide.
luna: The leaders admit that they led their followers astray; it reverses the section's good herd-leader who guides those behind him.

luna: The parable counts one man's ninety-nine ewes against another's single ewe and depicts an oppressive claim to another's flock; it complicates the section's simple relation between herd and owner.
terra: David recognizes that asking to add one ewe to ninety-nine is wrongdoing. The 38:23 flock dispute becomes a moral limit on a stronger owner's claim.
terra: David is made a successor and warned not to follow desire, lest it lead him astray from God's way. A human leader must himself remain guided.
terra: God creates eight mates of livestock and fashions humans in womb stages. The herd is presented as ordered pairs under the same creator who forms hidden human life.

luna: The parable contrasts one person divided among quarrelsome owners with one belonging to a single owner; it illuminates the section's statement that a herd has a master. | terra: A man belonging to quarrelling partners is contrasted with one belonging wholly to one man. This turns the source's single herd owner into a sharp image of undivided lordship.
terra: The believing man in Pharaoh's family says, “Follow me; I will guide you to the way of right conduct.” It is an exact human leader-and-followers counterpart to the source's hâdî.

luna: This ayah says livestock were created for people to ride and eat, directly supporting the section's picture of owned, useful animals. | terra: Cattle are made so people ride some and eat some. The source's two functions—carrying and benefit—are stated together.

luna: This ayah adds uses, journeys, and carrying loads by livestock and ships; it makes the section's load-bearing animal a shared Qur'anic scene. | terra: Beyond riding and eating, livestock carry people to needs held within their hearts. It gives the source's burden-bearing scene an inward as well as geographic destination.
terra: Thamud are given guidance but prefer blindness to it. Their choice places the source's camel-owning community on the side of refusing direction.
terra: God makes mates for people and for cattle and multiplies them by that order. The verse gives the herd's continuity a created, measured form.
terra: God creates and disperses living creatures through the heavens and earth, and can gather them when He wills. The wild herd's apparent freedom is set inside a larger divine power to gather.
terra: The Prophet is said to guide to a straight path. This turns the source's request for a leading guide into the messenger's active function.

luna: This ayah joins a habitable earth, roads, and guidance, paralleling the section's move from a settled pasture to the request to be led on a path. | terra: God makes paths in the earth “so that you may be guided”; 43:12 then supplies mounts. The adjacent route makes riding animals part of a guided journey.

luna: This ayah names livestock among the paired things made for riding, a direct scene of animals placed in human service. | terra: God creates pairs and makes ships and an'am for riding. It directly develops the source's binek as a creature made to carry its rider.

luna: The ayah describes settling on the backs of subdued animals and remembering the Lord; it joins the section's tamed mount to its language of divine ownership. | terra: Settling on the animals' backs and remembering the One who subjected them gives the source's tame mount an explicit act of riding and acknowledgment of its true owner.

luna: The riding passage ends by returning to the Lord; this ayah's contribution is to place the animal journey under the same Lord named as owner in the section. | terra: After riding the subjected animals, people remember their Lord and their return to Him. This gives the source's mount a rider's verbal acknowledgment of its owner.
terra: Pharaoh makes his people compliant and they obey him. It is a false human herd-leader: obedience follows a deceiving ruler rather than a trustworthy guide.
terra: Jesus says that Allah is his Rabb and theirs, so they should worship Him; this is a straight path. Rabb, service, and route appear in the relation the section develops.
terra: The jinn hear a scripture that guides to truth and to a straight path. It makes the guide a heard revelation that can lead a responsive group.
terra: Disbelievers eat and enjoy as cattle eat, while the Fire is their lodging. The source's animal benefit becomes a warning against human life reduced to unguided consumption.
terra: Those who are guided receive increased guidance and their piety. The ayah depicts guidance as a path that can deepen for those who stay with it.
terra: Some turn back after guidance has become clear, following Satan's inducement. This is a human version of departing from a recognized guide.

luna: The ayah says hypocrites can be recognized by their marks (root و س م); this is another human-status use of the identifying-mark root named for the camel brand. | terra: Hypocrites could be known by their marks and by the tone of speech. The source's identifying wasm becomes a moral sign that exposes a hidden affiliation.
terra: The hady is held back from reaching its place. Against the source's leader and followed route, this is a concrete animal offering stopped short of its destination.

luna: The ayah describes a mark on believers' faces (root و س م); the sign parallels the source's identifying camel brand while marking devotion rather than ownership. | terra: The believers have a sīmā on their faces from prostration. It gives the source's recognition-mark a devotional rather than proprietary form.
terra: The Prophet is declared neither astray nor misled. A true guide is first distinguished from the source's dallīn.
terra: People follow only conjecture and desire though guidance has come from their Lord. It names a rival following that leaves the received route.
terra: Thamud refuse to follow a single man from among them and call the result error. Their rhetoric reverses the source's herd that needs an acknowledged leader to follow.

luna: The she-camel is sent as a trial and people are told to watch; this makes the camel a possession and sign under divine authority. | terra: The she-camel is sent as a test. It gives the animal a divinely assigned status, unlike the source's camel whose owner is unknown.

luna: The water is divided between the people and the she-camel; the ayah adds an explicit limit on human use of an animal's shared pasture environment. | terra: Water is divided between the people and the she-camel, with each drinking turn attended. 54:27 names the camel; this ayah gives its concrete share at the herd's water source.

luna: The people call their companion, who hamstrings the she-camel; the act reverses the care and restraint around a herd animal. | terra: They call their companion, who seizes and hamstrings the she-camel. Harm to the named animal reverses the protected grazing relation in the source.

luna: The criminals are recognized by their marks (root و س م); as with the camel brand, a visible sign identifies its bearer, though here it signals guilt. | terra: Criminals are recognized by their marks before being seized. The source's visible identifier is recast as recognition in judgment.
terra: Those charged with Torah but not carrying it are compared to a donkey carrying books. The burden-bearing animal exposes a human failure to be led by what it carries.
terra: The earth is made compliant, people walk its paths and eat its provision. The source's tamed animal is broadened to a tamed terrain that carries its walkers along routes.
terra: It contrasts one who walks fallen on his face with one who walks upright on a straight path. The bodily route makes the source's guided-versus-stray movement visible.
terra: God threatens to brand a denier on the snout. The source's recognition brand on a camel becomes its fearful contrary: a public mark of disgrace.
terra: The jinn say they heard a wondrous Qur'an that guides to right conduct. The source's requested direction is here received by a community and followed in belief.
terra: Those who hear guidance divide into Muslims who seek right conduct and deviators who become fuel. It states a collective fork between following and going crooked.
terra: Had people remained on the straight way, they would have been given abundant water. The route is linked to provision in a way that recalls pasture and watering.

luna: The fleeing donkeys give the section's wild-donkey herd a direct animal scene, while their flight from a lion reverses the calm movement of a herd following its guide. | terra: The rejecters are likened to startled wild asses. This uses the source's wild-donkey herd sense to picture a human refusal to heed a summons.

luna: This ayah identifies the donkeys of 74:50 as fleeing from a lion; that detail completes the wild-herd image with the danger they flee. | terra: Their wild-asses image is completed by flight from a lion. The animal group's panicked dispersal sharpens the source's contrast between being led and running loose.
terra: God shows the human the way, leaving gratitude or denial open. The source's guided herd image becomes a morally answerable human route.
terra: The sparks are likened to yellow camels. The concrete camel's color and mass are turned into an image of the Fire, not a herd under care.

luna: This ayah explicitly brings out the earth's water and pasture, matching the section's valued grazing ground. | terra: God brings out the earth's water and pasture; 79:33 identifies that created order as provision for people and their cattle. This ayah contributes the grazing ground itself.
terra: The earth's water, pasture, and mountains are made provision for people and their an'am. It directly places the herd's grazing world within measured provision.
terra: Pasture is brought forth amid the food sequence. This is the source's otlak as a created element of the herd's place.

luna: This ayah names pasture as provision for people and their livestock, making explicit who benefits from the grazing land in the section. | terra: The preceding vegetation is expressly “provision for you and your cattle”; 80:31 supplies the pasture and this ayah states its shared purpose.
luna: The pregnant camels left unattended reverse the section's cared-for, owned herd and its lost camel; here even valuable camels are neglected.

luna: This ayah gathers wild beasts immediately after the neglected camels of 81:4, completing the section's striking contrast between abandoned domestic animals and wild herds. | terra: Wild beasts are gathered. The source's wild, ownerless-looking herds meet an eschatological gathering under a power none of them escapes.
terra: God creates and proportionates; 87:3 then says He determines and guides. The ayah contributes the making-fit side of the source's guide-and-creature image.
terra: God creates, proportionates, determines, and guides. The source's hâdî is extended from an animal at the front to the Creator's fitting and directing of creatures.

luna: This ayah brings forth pasture; 87:5 immediately shows it becoming dark debris, extending the section's valued grazing ground into a cycle of change. | terra: Immediately after divine guidance, God brings forth pasture. The sequence makes guidance and grazing part of one ordering of creaturely life.

luna: The pasture of 87:4 becomes dark debris in this ayah; the scene reverses the section's favored grazing place by showing its later disappearance. | terra: The pasture of 87:4 is then made dark debris. Its change limits any reading of the grazing ground as self-sustaining or permanent.

luna: The ayah asks people to look at how camels were created; it directs attention to the same animal whose carrying body, mark, and domestication the section examines. | terra: The camel itself is set before the reader as a created sign. It lets the section's concrete camel remain an object of contemplation rather than only a lexical illustration.
terra: The human is shown the two paths. It gives a compact counterpart to the source's one leading route and the possibility of going loose from it.

luna: The people are warned about God's she-camel and her drink; this links the animal's ownership to a protected share of water. | terra: The messenger names “Allah's she-camel” and her watering turn. Divine possession and a camel's allotted access to water directly answer the source's ownerless-versus-owned camel.

luna: The people deny the warning and hamstring the she-camel, a direct reversal of leaving a known animal in safety. | terra: They deny the messenger and hamstring her; the preceding 91:13 names Allah's she-camel and watering, while this ayah records the violation and its consequence.
terra: “Upon Us is guidance” identifies the true source of the direction for which the section asks.

luna: The ayah uses ḍāllan and then says God guided; it gives the section's lost-animal image a precise Qur'anic movement from being lost to receiving guidance, while leaving their contexts distinct. | terra: The addressee is found in need of direction and then guided. It is the personal movement out of the source's dalālah scene.
terra: The command to speak of the Lord's ni'mah makes the source's benefit vocabulary an act of acknowledgment rather than mere possession.
terra: “Rabb of people” transfers the source's owner-and-nurturer title from the herd image to the human community seeking protection.
terra: “Malik of people,” beside 114:1, repeats the source's two owner titles over one human flock-like community.
